title: Night people
hookLine: those who turn night into day are living backwards (Letters 122)

cards: It's 1:40 in the morning. The phone is a small sun on your face. You meant to sleep an hour ago, and somehow you're watching a stranger restore a rusty knife.
Letter 122 opens in autumn. The days are getting shorter, and Seneca says a good person still gets up early, as if to borrow back the light.
Then he turns to a set of Romans who did the opposite on purpose: wealthy people who slept through the day, dined at midnight, went to bed at dawn, and thought it made them interesting.

teach.b: First, antipodes in the same city. Seneca borrows a joke from old Cato: there are people who have never once seen the sun rise or set.
Seneca calls them antipodes, the people imagined living on the underside of the earth, except these live on the underside of the same street.

teach.h: PEDO TELLS TIME BY THE NOISE.
teach.b: Second, the neighbor you could tell time by. A storyteller named Pedo told Seneca about a man next door who lived entirely backwards.

Pedo could tell the hour of the night by the sounds coming over the wall: the accounts being read, the singing practice, the carriage being readied, all while the rest of Rome slept. Third, why they did it. Not for work.
It was a fashion. Doing what everyone else does felt cheap; reversing the clock got you noticed.

teach.h: A VICE THAT WANTS TO BE TALKED ABOUT.
teach.b: Seneca calls it a vice that wants to be talked about. Living against nature, he says, is like wanting roses in winter or drinking on an empty stomach: the effort is the point. Fourth, a fair word for night workers.

teach.h: NOT THE NIGHT SHIFT: THE IDLE NIGHT.
teach.b: Seneca's target is the luxury of it, not the nurse on a night shift, the baker, the parent up with a baby.
Those people aren't living backwards. They're carrying the night so others can sleep. His question is for the rest of us, awake at 1:40 for no reason we could name.

how: Some people who practice Stoic living keep a regular bedtime and an early start, treating the hours of light as the natural frame for their day, as Seneca urges in Letter 122.

games.q: you're a wealthy Roman. everyone dines at sunset. how do you get noticed, by Seneca's account?
o: sleep all day and dine at midnight.
games.why: some did exactly that, and Seneca calls it a vice that wants to be talked about: living backwards.

practice: Look at tonight before it arrives, and name the hour that would give you enough sleep, and the thing most likely to steal it: the phone, a show, one more task.

Picture yourself at that hour putting it down, in another room if you can, and lying in the dark with nothing left to prove. If your work keeps you up at night, picture your own rest instead, whatever hour it comes.

wordCard.voice: Night people. In Letter 122, Romans who slept by day and feasted by night to be noticed. Seneca calls it living backwards. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin from Greek, 'opposite-footed': Seneca's name for Romans who lived by night.

carryVoice: Your line: with the sun. Even in autumn, a good day borrows back the light. Day four hundred eighty-eight, done.
